content: Conductors must be selected based on the Minimum Circuit Ampacity (MCA), and switches must be chosen according to the Maximum Overcurrent Protection (MOP). The data provided by the mechanical discipline during the design phase may not be the final version. Due to potential discrepancies between the initially selected equipment and the actual procured equipment—especially in government tenders where manufacturers are not specified—different manufacturers may have varying power requirements for the same equipment. Therefore, during the IFC stage, the drawings must be updated based on the final procured equipment’s nameplate data and submitted documentation to produce the final IFC or construction version.

Control requirements are a common area of coordination challenges between electrical and mechanical disciplines. For example, whether equipment requires motor starters, Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs), or local control panels, as well as remote control functionality, must be clarified. This serves as a reminder, and it is recommended to pay special attention to this section.

When designing domestically, I initially worked alone as well. Although I had been in the design field for several years, it wasn’t until I personally took charge of the Building Automation Control System project and participated in multiple overseas design cases that I truly understood how to collaborate with other disciplines.

Additionally, is it necessary to disconnect the switch? The decision to disconnect depends on the equipment conditions and requires on-site installation. Regarding equipment usage modes—such as whether multiple ovens operate simultaneously, are arranged randomly during normal operation, or adopt a one-standby-one-active configuration—these operational modes must be confirmed with relevant stakeholders.

In North America, Louis Kuhn is typically designed by the mechanical section, as is the IT portion.

To conserve energy, we use equipment sensors to control lighting and air conditioning systems. For example, when occupants leave a room, the air conditioning system will automatically shut off. However, this application is not yet widespread, whereas lighting control is more common. Additionally, the airflow rate of air conditioning units (e.g., 2000 CFM and 15000 CFM) directly determines whether a duct smoke detector needs to be installed. In the event of a fire, it is also necessary to consider whether certain air conditioning units should be shut down.

Sprinkler system drawings include system diagrams and floor plans. System diagrams illustrate how the system is connected, while floor plans indicate the locations of equipment. Components that require coordinated monitoring in this system include the FM system, control valves, temperature switches, and flow switches. For dry and wet systems, an air compressor is also required. Furthermore, the power supply for fire pumps involves the emergency power supply.

The smoke control system must ensure power supply using emergency power and be interconnected with the fire protection system, including the placement of fans, fire dampers, and smoke dampers. Another critical requirement is electric heat tracing (EHT). In cold regions such as Canada and the U.S., winter temperatures can drop below freezing. If underground parking areas lack heating systems and use wet sprinkler systems, the water in the pipes may freeze. In such cases, electric heat tracing cables must be wrapped around the fire protection pipes for heating—a technique known as heat trace technology. This needs to be coordinated with the Mechanical Engineering Department. If a dry system is adopted, no trace heating is required; if a wet system is used and the parking lot is unheated, trace heating must be installed.

This needs to be coordinated with the Mechanical Engineering Department. If a dry system is adopted, no trace heating is required; if a wet system is used and the parking lot is unheated, trace heating must be installed.

The Electrical Engineering Department is responsible for designing the trace heating. While the Mechanical Engineering Department may provide input, trace heating design falls under the scope of the Electrical Engineering Department. However, the requirements for temperature control and related specifications are defined by the Mechanical Engineering Department.

The following are our requirements for the Mechanical Engineering Department.

For example, our electrical spaces include substations, electrical rooms, communication rooms, generator rooms, and UPS rooms. The primary environmental control requirement for these spaces is temperature, while humidity typically requires no special attention. Electrical rooms generate heat when equipped with numerous variable frequency drives (VFDs) and UPS units, and transformers also produce heat during operation. The heat dissipation efficiency of transformers usually ranges between 2% and 5%, meaning a 1,000 kVA transformer can generate 20 to 50 kW of heat—equivalent to a large electric heater. In summer, this continuous heat output can cause a significant rise in indoor temperatures, necessitating ventilation or cooling systems to maintain the ambient temperature in electrical rooms and substations.

Data centers, due to their high server density, exhibit even more pronounced heat generation. Unlike incandescent bulbs, which convert all electrical energy into light, servers transform 60% to 80% of their power consumption into heat, requiring air conditioning systems designed for such thermal loads. Additionally, it is critical to prevent severe clashes between electrical conduits and mechanical systems. In electrical rooms, the layout of air conditioning ducts and electrical conduits must be coordinated, while mechanical rooms involve power supply challenges for large equipment, such as the installation of switchboards and control panels.

The routing of pipelines in public areas is more complex, requiring alignment among electrical, plumbing, and HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) systems. This coordination is particularly crucial in residential projects with limited ceiling heights. Currently, large-scale projects often employ BIM technology to prevent spatial conflicts between systems. It is important to note that electrical spaces are not limited to electrical rooms but also encompass substations, generator rooms, and other similar areas.

We do not want pipes to pass through, with the exception of fire sprinkler pipelines. Dry and wet fire suppression systems are a different matter. Additionally, there are detailed coordination issues in ceiling spaces. For example, the ceiling must integrate lighting fixtures, fire detectors, HVAC ductwork (including return air ducts and supply air ducts), and the sprinkler system.

After our electrical and mechanical drawings are individually finalized, conflicts often arise when they are overlaid. Such issues must be resolved through professional coordination during the design phase; otherwise, clashes between mechanical and electrical systems will occur during on-site installation.

For the backup power system, generators involve not only electrical equipment but also fuel systems, gas systems, and supporting ventilation and exhaust facilities. Furthermore, mechanical considerations such as noise control and vibration elimination must be addressed. Underground parking areas require special attention to environmental control, primarily for vehicle exhaust treatment.

The system is equipped with air quality monitoring functionality, capable of detecting in real-time whether harmful gases in the parking lot exceed standard limits. Once levels are exceeded, the ventilation system will automatically activate to expel polluted air and introduce fresh air.

Regarding heat trace design and boundary of scope of work, there are numerous overlapping areas between the mechanical and electrical disciplines. For example:

- The equipment power-off switch shall be provided by the mechanical discipline.
- Duct smoke detectors shall be installed by the electrical discipline and supplied as part of the electrical equipment package.
- Variable frequency drives (VFDs) shall be supplied, installed, and commissioned by the electrical discipline.
- Control wiring construction shall be carried out by the electrical discipline, with mechanical discipline providing interface requirements and coordination.

These issues require clear delineation of responsibilities between consultants and contractors to avoid omissions or duplication of work.

These issues require clear delineation of responsibilities between consultants and contractors to avoid omissions or duplication of work.

Additionally, when electrical equipment rooms are located in basements, waterproofing must be considered. The mechanical discipline must incorporate drainage design, including features like drainage channels, to prevent water accumulation in electrical equipment rooms. The architectural discipline should also participate in coordination to ensure clear interfaces between all disciplines’ work.

The main focus involves power supply requirements, such as equipment like elevators and parking lot roller doors, which are specified by the client, thus necessitating clarity on their power supply requirements. Additionally, lighting and electrical system designs must be based on the floor plan and ceiling plan.

It is essential to understand the floor-to-floor height, ceiling type, and wall construction, the latter of which relates to conduit routing issues, including wall thickness and fireproofing requirements. The design of fire compartments must also be considered as it affects conduit layout.

Regarding door hardware, it is necessary to specify which areas require electronic access control systems. Finally, electrical load information serves as a critical design basis.

We need to clarify the following requirements: spatial dimensions, layout method, floor height, ceiling type (e.g., electrical equipment rooms typically do not have ceilings or require specific heights such as 3.6 meters or 3.3 meters), door specifications (single or double doors), and the number of exits. Additionally, indoor and outdoor lighting solutions need to be considered, including special requirements for decorative lighting, luminaire selection, and lighting control strategies.

Regarding the elevator machine room location selection, relevant technical specifications must be obtained. When designing the access control system, coordination with emergency evacuation routes is required. For the integrated ceiling layout plan, collaboration between the MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) and architectural disciplines is involved, typically led and coordinated by the architectural discipline; if there is no architectural discipline participation, the MEP discipline will be responsible for coordination.

When used in conjunction with elevators, coordination with public facilities must also be considered. For example, generators or PMTs can be deployed on-site for coordinated use—here specifically referring to outdoor equipment—whose location and dimensional requirements must be clearly defined.

Additionally, the position of electrical spaces, fire protection requirements, equipment layout, and sealing time parameters must be provided. Regarding data centers, sometimes the floor needs to be raised to accommodate IT equipment (such as servers), with electrical conduits or ventilation systems installed in the mezzanine. If such requirements exist, they should be specified accordingly.

Special attention should also be given to equipment such as large distribution panels.

Regarding the installation location of electrical equipment, domestic practices usually address it on-site, especially for equipment installed at later stages, such as drilling holes. However, for distribution panels installed on concrete walls, positions must be reserved in advance on the drawings. Coordination is particularly crucial for surface-mounted equipment and electrical shafts, requiring clear dimensions, locations, and vertical alignment.

Some electrical equipment needs to be installed in basements, outdoor areas, or low-lying zones. It is recommended to elevate the equipment by approximately 15 cm to prevent water ingress. Sufficient space must be reserved for the installation, transportation, and future replacement of large electrical equipment.

For cables passing through roofs or exterior walls, waterproofing measures must be implemented. When conduits penetrate firewalls, the application of fireproof coatings should be handled by the relevant parties. Additionally, coordination with the structural discipline is necessary to meet related requirements.

Structural coordination is relatively straightforward, primarily involving the arrangement of heavy electrical equipment. If the equipment is placed on a floor slab without a basement underneath, no special treatment is required. However, if the floor slab is suspended below, parameters such as weight and area must be provided.

Additionally, coordination is needed when incoming lines penetrate the foundation. The Po foundation in streetlight design also requires coordination.

The installation of heavy electrical equipment (such as luminaires and distribution panels), including suspended CableTree or wall-mounted transformers, C-Link installations, etc., all require coordination with structural engineers to ensure structural safety. Simultaneously, relevant coordination with the cable discipline is also necessary.

For example, Cable primarily refers to the external components of a building. Within a site, certain equipment such as water pumps and sewage pumps require power supply. Furthermore, since Cable work involves creating site plans, electrical equipment installed outdoors—like generators or switchgear—also needs corresponding support.

Cable work sometimes requires indicating street lighting on drawings, so relevant documentation must be provided. Coordination is necessary for the comprehensive layout and intersection alignment of underground utilities. If a site contains numerous electrical conduits and manholes used for cable pulling or installation, these must be coordinated with the Cable discipline.

Tasks such as trench excavation, backfilling, and cable procurement must clearly define the responsible parties and be noted in the respective drawings to ensure alignment between contractors during construction. Coordination with landscape designers is also required.

The collaboration with landscape architects is relatively limited, primarily involving the electrical design for landscape lighting. Landscape lighting fixtures may come with built-in photo sensors or may require centralized photo sensors to achieve automatic illumination at dusk.

The designers will provide a layout plan or specific locations for the landscape lighting, based on which we design the power supply network. Additionally, if outdoor equipment such as generators, transformers, or switchgear is involved, their placement must align with the overall aesthetic of the landscape design, including the arrangement of street lights.

At the same time, coordination with other consultant teams is also required.

For example, data centers in theaters, hospitals, or other nuclear facilities are not designed by architects but by program designers specializing in these industries. These professionals are familiar with the specific design requirements of these specialized fields, and we need to work closely with them.

Since they provide equipment lists and detailed processes, we must fully understand this information and coordinate effectively with contractors.

During the construction phase, depending on the contract terms, we may chair construction meetings, or the meetings may be chaired by the client or the contractor.

We need to review documents such as construction drawings, site instructions, change orders, and payment certificates. The workflow during this phase is largely similar to our collaboration with the client throughout the construction period, so it won’t be elaborated further.

At this stage, we also need to coordinate the work between the client and the contractor.

Coordination between manufacturers and suppliers primarily involves the following aspects.

At this stage, we also need to coordinate the work between both the client and the contractor.

Coordination between manufacturers and suppliers primarily involves the following aspects.

From a consulting perspective, the first step is to understand the budget price for each piece of equipment or system during the design phase, which is mainly used for construction budgeting. If budgeting is unnecessary, this information may be omitted. Large-scale projects are typically handled by specialized firms, while small to medium-sized consulting projects still require a general price range (ballpark number).

Secondly, when selecting systems, technical documentation must be obtained from suppliers, including specifications (specs), data sheets (containing dimensions, weight, capacity, etc.). As consultants, it is also essential to ascertain the lead time for large electrical equipment or complex systems to ensure alignment with the construction schedule.

Additionally, access to technical support is crucial, as engineers cannot be experts in all equipment and systems. Manufacturers must provide specialized assistance, such as lighting calculations or generator sizing. They often offer high-quality technical literature, given their deeper expertise in product and equipment details.

Finally, during construction, installation, and commissioning, manufacturer collaboration is required for system startup. The key challenge lies in achieving this effective coordination.

During construction, installation, and commissioning, manufacturer collaboration is required for system startup. The key challenge lies in achieving this effective coordination.

First, we need to familiarize ourselves with and learn as much as possible about other knowledge related to the electrical engineering field, while simultaneously enhancing our professional skills and expertise. In North America, we frequently organize “launcher learn” activities, where manufacturers are invited during lunch breaks to introduce their products, combining dining with learning. This approach is both time-efficient and highly effective, and many manufacturers are happy to participate in such events.

Second, we need to summarize the lessons learned from past projects, known as “Project lesson learned,” to avoid repeating the same mistakes in future work. Additionally, it is essential to strengthen QA/QC (Quality Assurance/Quality Control) efforts, paying close attention to drawing approvals and peer reviews during the review process. At the same time, emphasis should be placed on documentation management, ensuring that all communications with stakeholders are recorded. This allows for traceability in case of issues and protects our interests.

Furthermore, it is crucial to understand the requirements of local Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) and utility companies, as well as to have a clear grasp of the entire project workflow and its requirements. During project execution, it is necessary to track any changes that occur, as these often involve financial implications, and proper paperwork must be maintained.

The first case is a university performing arts center located within its office building. With a project budget of approximately $50 million, the design fee alone reached $7 million. Multiple consultant teams were involved, including theater process designers, architectural concept designers, detail designers, and architects responsible for the theater’s exterior design. Additionally, there were specialized designers for theater lighting, stage curtain control systems, as well as sound and audiovisual effects. These consultant teams hailed from the United States and Canada.

My company was responsible for civil engineering and MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) design, and I served as the electrical coordinator for this project. Given the theater’s specialized requirements for lighting and audiovisual effects, professional theater lighting designers and stage control system designers were also engaged.

This is a large-scale industrial liquid pipeline project involving a petroleum transmission pipeline system. The project includes multiple pump stations (Terminals), each equipped with facilities such as oil pipes, pipelines, and pressure pumps. Industrial projects of this nature typically incur high costs, and I was responsible for three to four sub-projects, each with a budget ranging between $50 million and $100 million.

The project was exceptionally well-managed, as evidenced by the following key aspects:

Detailed Design: The design was highly meticulous. Although the design fees were substantial, they ensured the project’s quality.

Smooth Coordination: Collaboration among the client, consultants, and contractors was highly efficient, with all parties working seamlessly together.

Low Change Rate: The project’s change orders accounted for only 5%, significantly lower than the industry average of 15%-30%.

The project strictly adhered to Western management practices and processes as followed in Canada. With an experienced and well-managed team, it was recognized as the second successful case study.

At that time, there were two renovation projects for a pulp mill in Vancouver. I was not involved in the preliminary design and only completed 60% of the design work. Construction had already begun when a friend, as the company’s responsible person, encountered difficulties and invited me to take over the project.

The project was initiated after Indonesian Chinese pulp company APP acquired the factory in Canada. Eager for quick results, they rushed into construction with only 60% of the design completed, attempting to operate using models like MBO. However, since contractors had to comply with local regulations, the lack of design coordination and the team’s inexperience ultimately led to high costs.

The total investment for the project was approximately 100–200 million CAD, with the electrical engineering budget doubling from an initial 6 million to 12 million CAD—a 100% overrun. The main issues stemmed from neglecting the coordination between design and construction, as well as unfamiliarity with local contractors’ workflows and legal environment. Project managers were from Taiwan and applied domestic or Southeast Asian management practices. However, in North America, owners and contractors operate on equal footing, rendering the traditional “client calls the shots” approach ineffective. Contractors have the right to reject unreasonable demands, leaving owners helpless even when facing high loan interest rates.

A similar situation occurred in the Dalian Comprehensive Service Building for the Disabled project. Approaches used in China proved ineffective overseas. As observed in the Canadian oil project, an Italian oil company also suffered losses in Alberta due to a lack of understanding of local conditions. This underscores the importance of the Chinese principle, “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.” Many Chinese developers in the Vancouver area have paid the price for this lesson.

In the process of participating in development projects or conducting business, everyone inevitably needs to pay a certain price. Of course, if you can fully understand the relevant circumstances in advance, you can avoid unnecessary detours.
